newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong pension plan seems to win Tung's support.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong pension plan seems to win Tung's support.

text.p: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's chief executive-designate, suggested on Friday that Hong Kong's pension plan has his support.
The so-called Mandatory Provident Fund will require all working Hong Kong people and employers to contribute to an annual pension fund.

"Hong Kong needs to provide an adequate safety net for those who are aged and less fortunate. In this respect, although somewhat late, Hong Kong is working on a Mandatory Provident Fund," Tung told a meeting of central bankers and finance ministers in Hong Kong.
The MPF, as it is known in Hong Kong, will require both employers and employees to contribute five percent of the worker's salary into an authorised pension fund.
Tung said the MPF, which could be subject to a 70-percent foreign currency restriction, would support the development of regional bond markets while upholding traditional Chinese values.
"In this way we can create a social fabric that combines the best of the East and West, and this will make our society strong and cohesive," he said.
China has not yet expressed an opinion on the MPF, which is still being debated by Hong Kong's Legislative Council, the elected body that will be dismantled on July 1.
In the past, China has attacked welfare initiatives launched by departing colonial governor Chris Patten.
Tung's comments follow Thursday's release of the Hong Kong government's spending estimates in advance of the March 12 budget, which covers the year the territory returns to China.
The estimates revealed a slowdown in welfare spending, to HK$19.4 billion in the coming year. This represents a 9.4 percent increase in welfare spending compared to last year's 14.7-percent rise.

"We in Hong Kong must ensure that our people are proud to be part of the community," Tung said. "This means we have to provide them with a decent standard living such as adequate housing, a clean environment and a satisfying way of life with cultural stimulation and personal freedom. How we achieve this in a changing environment and with the strict budgetary discipline will be one of the greatest challenges of the SAR government."
